passage: At the tube-well after school, Vishal was still buzzing about the block-level maths quiz. "Rajni, you were amazing! Honestly, you think like a boy," he said, grinning, and held up his hand for a high five. Rajni didn't lift hers. "What does that mean?" "It's a compliment! Girls usually..." He stopped. Her face had gone very still. "Usually what?" she asked quietly, and picked up her bucket. Vishal walked home with his cheeks burning. He had meant it as the best praise he knew. At dinner he told his mother, who put down her ladle. "Would you like it if someone said you were clever for a boy?" Vishal stared at his roti. He hadn't thought of it like that at all.

qa.q: Which quiz was Vishal still excited about?
qa.a: The block-level maths quiz.

qa.q: Why were Vishal's cheeks burning on the walk home?
qa.a: He was embarrassed and confused; he had meant it as the best praise he knew and was shocked that it hurt Rajni.

qa.q: What could Vishal do the next day at the tube-well?
qa.a: He could tell Rajni she was amazing, full stop, and say sorry that "like a boy" made it sound as if girls usually aren't.

qa.q: How might Rajni have heard "you think like a boy"?
qa.a: Rajni likely heard that her win was an exception for a girl, which takes the credit away from her own mind.

grounding: A teenager compliments a girl by saying she thinks like a boy, sincerely meaning it kindly, and is shocked to learn it hurt.

passage: In the school library in Edinburgh, Freya leaned over to Alejandro's table with a warm smile. "I just wanted to say, you're honestly so inspiring. Like, just coming to school every day in your wheelchair." Alejandro looked up from his chemistry. "I come to school to do chemistry. Same as you." "No, I mean, it's brave." "It's a ramp and a lift," he said, not unkindly, and went back to his book. Freya's face went hot. She had rehearsed it on the bus, sure it would make his day. On the walk home she replayed it: she'd praised him for existing, not for anything he'd done. That evening she messaged him: "Sorry about earlier. I meant it kindly, but I get why it landed wrong." He replied: "Thanks. You can say my titration was inspiring though."

qa.q: What was Alejandro studying in the library?
qa.a: He was studying chemistry.

qa.q: Why did Freya's face go hot?
qa.a: She was shocked and embarrassed; she had rehearsed the compliment, sure it would make his day, and it landed wrong.

qa.q: Which part of Freya's apology made it work?
qa.a: She didn't defend her intent or ask for comfort; she named that it landed wrong and said sorry.

qa.q: What might Alejandro's joke about his titration tell Freya?
qa.a: It suggests he's happy to be praised for what he actually does, and that things are still friendly between them.

grounding: A teenager praises a classmate in a wheelchair as inspiring for simply attending school, meaning it kindly, and learns the effect was not kind.

passage: In the study hall of the residential school, Damini leaned across the desk to read Lalremsiami's essay and gasped. "This is so good! Honestly, I thought sports-quota kids only cared about training." She laughed, meaning it as a compliment. Lalremsiami closed the notebook. "I'm in the reading club too. Since Class 6." "I know, I just meant..." "You meant you were surprised." The warden's bell rang for lights out. Damini lay awake on her bunk, stunned. She had been trying to be nice. She replayed the words and heard, for the first time, the "only" in them. In the morning she found Lalremsiami at the water cooler. "I'm sorry. I put you in a box. The essay's just good." Lalremsiami nodded slowly. "Okay. Thanks for coming back."

qa.q: Since when has Lalremsiami been in the reading club?
qa.a: Since Class 6.

qa.q: What was Damini feeling as she lay awake on her bunk?
qa.a: She was stunned and uneasy; she had meant to be nice and only now heard the "only" in her own words.

qa.q: What was the turning point for Damini, and what made her morning apology work?
qa.a: Hearing the "only" was the turning point; the apology worked because it named what she did, putting Lalremsiami in a box, without asking for reassurance.

qa.q: What might "Thanks for coming back" show about how Lalremsiami felt?
qa.a: Lalremsiami was hurt, but valued that Damini came back to own it instead of letting it slide.

grounding: A student compliments a classmate's essay through a stereotype about sports-quota students, meaning well, and is shocked to realise it hurt.

passage:
Sahil,
I tried to say this at the bus stop and it came out wrong, so I'm writing it.
At the science fair, when the judges praised your bridge, I said really loudly, "Obviously! It's in his blood. His family runs the cycle shop, he was born to fix things." I meant it as the biggest compliment. I was proud of you.
Then you didn't talk the whole ride home, and Tanya told me later what you'd said to her: that you spent three weeks on the load calculations, and I made it sound like your hands did it and your head didn't.
Honestly, I didn't see it. I was shocked. I kept thinking, but I was being nice!
Being nice and landing nice aren't the same thing, I get that now. The calculations were yours. I'm sorry I made it about the shop.
Hemant

qa.q: How long did Sahil spend on the load calculations?
qa.a: Three weeks.

qa.q: Why was Hemant so shocked to learn the comment had hurt?
qa.a: Hemant sincerely meant "it's in his blood" as the biggest compliment and felt proud, so it came as a real surprise that it had erased Sahil's hard thinking.

qa.q: At the fair, what could Hemant have chosen to say instead?
qa.a: Hemant could have praised the actual work, something like "Sahil did all the load calculations", instead of tying the bridge to the family's cycle shop.

qa.q: How did the comment look from Sahil's side?
qa.a: To Sahil, three weeks of careful maths was turned into an inherited knack, as if the family shop mattered more than Sahil's own mind.

grounding: A student praises Sahil with a stereotype about the family trade, sincerely meaning it kindly, and is shocked to learn the effect hurt.

passage: Okay, Rukmini, you asked what I learnt this term, so here's the embarrassing one. I'm Gargi, and I'm the joker in our group, right? Everyone knows me for it. During the group project, Francis kept the only calculator on his desk, and I said, "Classic only child, never learnt to share," and did a little spoilt-baby voice. Everybody laughed. Francis laughed too, sort of. I thought that was the end of it. Two days later his friend told me Francis went home upset. Apparently he's heard that line since forever, and he's the one who photocopies his notes for half the class. I was honestly shocked. I kept saying, "But it was a joke! I like him!" And I do. That's the weird part. I meant it as teasing between friends, and it still landed as one more person calling him selfish. I said sorry the next morning, with no jokes attached.

qa.q: What did Gargi say when Francis kept the calculator?
qa.a: "Classic only child, never learnt to share," in a little spoilt-baby voice.

qa.q: What does Gargi's "But it was a joke! I like him!" show about how Gargi felt?
qa.a: Gargi was genuinely shocked and a bit defensive, because the joke came from affection and Gargi never imagined it could feel like an insult.

qa.q: What turning point shows Gargi learning, and what made the apology work?
qa.a: Gargi apologised the next morning with no jokes attached, which took the hurt seriously instead of explaining the good intent again.

qa.q: What is it like for Francis to hear the only-child line once more?
qa.a: Francis has heard it forever, so even from a friend it feels like one more person calling him selfish, despite sharing notes with half the class.

grounding: A teenager teases a friend with an only-child stereotype, sure it is friendly, and is shocked to discover the joke hurt.
